translations.text: “MY SHEEP,” says the giver of life, “hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life.” What else can one expect from life but life? What other hope can one receive from light but the rays of light? Or what else can one expect from the fountain of blessings but the goodness of its gifts? Therefore David also says, “With you is the fountain of life, and by the light of your face we see light.” That light is pure and spreads by its nature, sending out many and varied rays of goodness. For it heals the various afflictions of souls and cures the various pains of bodies, because he is the creator of bodies and souls. Just as he granted them a single creation, so he also bestows a single healing. And we can learn from today’s reading how the fountain of good things possesses goodness in himself.

Jesus came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had turned the water into wine. Remember yesterday’s words: whatever is said in bodily terms must not be understood in bodily terms. Jesus came, not through a change in the power of his divinity, but through his body’s movement from place to place. For if his nature is unlimited in its divinity, then he is everywhere. He appears in the body sometimes here and sometimes there, carrying out the order of the divine plan, not changing in his nature. Jesus came and experienced weariness. He grew weary, not in his divine nature, but in his humanity. “Jesus came,” it says, “and was weary from the journey.” He grew weary in that which was capable of weariness, and not in his divinity, which never experiences weariness. The prophet also bears witness: “The eternal God,” he says, “who formed the ends of the earth, will neither hunger nor grow weary.” Yet here it says that he grew weary and hungered. “He fasted,” it says, “for forty days and forty nights, and afterward he hungered.” And it is clear that he hungered when he willed to do so. You see that the divine nature is free from needs, and that, according to the divine plan, he grows weary and hungers in the body.

And this is what is amazing: he grows weary so that he may give rest to the weary. “Come to me, you who are weary, and I will give you rest.” You see, then, that according to his divinity he gives rest to our weary nature, and according to his providential care he recognizes the needs of our humanity. Was he not able to move through the air the holy body which he took from us for our salvation, so that it would not suffer weariness? And did he not do something like this when he carried Habakkuk’s body from the land of Palestine to Babylon in a single instant? Through angelic grace he transported a man, a prophet, from one land to another; he suffered no weariness and felt no exertion. And could not the power of God himself grant his own body as much as the angel’s hand was able to accomplish? But there the necessities of the situation demanded speed, for in Babylon there was no worshiper of God to feed him. He saw that the prophet was in distress among the lions because he bore witness to the worship of God, and through an angel’s hand he seized the other prophet also and brought him there to that prophet. And see the wonder: it does not say that the angel carried him, but that he took him and set him there. See the angel’s power! Why are you astonished at the Creator of angels? He lifts and carries the prophet, not by supporting him beneath his feet and raising him upward, but by grasping his hair and snatching him away. And we know, brothers, how much pain the body suffers when someone is dragged by the hair. Yet the prophet crossed so many places and traveled so far, pulled by his hair, and suffered nothing; and in a single instant he took him and set him there. For it was an angel’s power, which not only lifted him but also granted lightness to his body. What was lifted was a body, but what lifted and carried it was a spirit. “He who made his angels spirits,” it says.

And do not be astonished that a light nature lifted a heavy body. First, even here among these created things that we can see, some things are heavy by nature, and some are light [?]. It does not depend on weight or size, but on the nature of created things, whatever they may be. Why is it that all the great trees—even if entire forests are cut down and fall into water—do not sink, while a great sea cannot keep one little needle, or a small [?] of iron, afloat? Thus it does not depend on size or weight, but on the Creator’s craftsmanship. Yet iron by itself has no means of remaining on the water, but with something light it stays on the water and is carried from place to place. They fill great ships with iron and take them wherever they wish; and because wood is light by nature, the light thing lifts the heavy thing. Take another example as well: a person cannot swim on the water for many hours, even if he knows the skill. Because he cannot keep exerting himself for long without resting, his arms grow weary, and he is forced to sink.

Just as a scorching wind first damages the root, and then the branches dry up along with it, so also in the worship of God: if the heart first becomes blind, then the fruit of the mouth dries up. However much the heretic’s tongue speaks slander, it becomes more and more unfruitful, as the prophet also says: “Ephraim’s head became diseased, and his root dried up, and he bears no fruit.” Yet one can often see outward forms of worship even among the enemies of the worship of God. There is a congregation in the church, and a congregation among the heretics; an altar here, and something called an altar there; true priests here, and false priests there. Here the gospel is believed, and there the gospel is mocked. Here the only-begotten Son of God is glorified, and there the only-begotten Son of God is treated as an enemy. Here the Holy Spirit rejoices in the flocks, and there the Holy Spirit is grieved by unbelief. For when the Holy Spirit sees ungodliness, he is grieved. For this reason Paul also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, by whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption.”

Now, when you see among the heretics outward forms of religion resembling those of the church, do not be deceived by their appearance, but examine the truth. The Egyptian magicians also imitated the deeds of Moses, but these were appearances, not truth. Moses threw his staff onto the ground, and it became a serpent. The magicians also threw down their staffs, and they became serpents. Their appearances were alike, but the truth revealed the distinction between them, for Moses’ staff swallowed their staffs, showing that falsehood is swallowed up by truth. And so that you may know, brother, that every heretical opposition that draws up its battle line against the words of the apostles belongs to the same company as those magicians, listen to Paul: “Those who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. But evil people and magicians will advance further into evil, being deceived and deceiving others. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: people whose minds are corrupted, unapproved in the faith.”

Pay close attention: he calls the opponents of the word of truth evil people and magicians. Why magicians? Because they deceive ignorant listeners, for the words of deceivers are sorcery to those who are deceived. For example, brothers, when people scratch their ears because they itch, scratching seems pleasant. But when they do it far too often, they cause sores, and the ears become deaf from the repeated scratching. Likewise, the words of heretics at first seem flattering to the ears, but afterward they deafen the senses. For this reason the apostle also says: “In the last times some will break away from the faith, following the itching of their ears.” What is this itching of the ears? Being deceived by fables. Everything the heretics say is fables. For this reason Paul also says: “They will turn their ears away from the truth and fall into fables.” Into which fables? Those of Arius, Macedonius, Montanus, the Manichaeans, and others like them, for they have all turned aside into fables and stand opposed to the truth. And he spoke not only of their opposition, but also of their breaking away. “But they will advance no further, for their foolishness will become apparent to everyone, as theirs also did.” We have the words of the apostles as pledges that put us on our guard. The physician of souls is a guarantor [?] with me, to dispel [?].

From now on, do not let the outward appearances of heretics who revile godliness deceive you. For among the Jews too, many had the outward forms of godliness, but there was no zeal for truth in them. Isaiah compares them to an unwatered garden and to a leafy tree in which there is no fruit. He says, “They shall be like a terebinth stripped of its leaves, and like an unwatered garden.” The community of heretics is also an unwatered garden. It is not watered by the water of life, of which the Giver of Life says, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scriptures say, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” Jesus said this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive.

See how they are an unwatered garden. He did not say, “Like a garden that does not know water,” but, “Like an unwatered garden.” They say that the Holy Spirit exists, but they do not have him. They preach, but they do not enjoy the gifts of the Spirit, for the Holy Spirit does not dwell in ungrateful souls. As long as godliness is in a person, the Holy Spirit dwells there; and when godliness departs, the Holy Spirit also departs. Indeed, we must conclude that all human souls receive either the Holy Spirit after grace or an unclean spirit. I do not mean that the Holy Spirit performs prophetic or apostolic works in a person. Rather, if someone does not have faith—for faith is a gift of the Spirit—he does not have the Holy Spirit. Even if someone is an insignificant layperson, indeed among the very least, and has only faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit is in him. No one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit. The soul must either be enlightened by the Holy Spirit or come under the power of unclean spirits. And who is there who would say this? When King Saul acted lawlessly and presumed to turn his mind to the unapproachable mystery, which it was not lawful for him to offer, he who had once slaughtered mediums and diviners then himself sought refuge with diviners. And what do the Scriptures say? “The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an unclean spirit tormented him.”

Heretics are an unwatered garden, and however many plants they plant, they are not reliable. Whoever follows not the voice of God but his own thoughts, even if he plants a plant, it is a plant of unbelief. Isaiah bears witness that anyone who does not have the word of God, even if he plants something, is not reliable and faithful. Just as there is a plant of faith, so there is also a plant of unbelief. All the plants of heretics are plants of unbelief, for their thoughts give birth to them. And every right glorification according to the Gospel and the apostles is a plant of faith and reliable seed. Therefore the Giver of Life also said concerning the Jews, “Leave them alone. Every plant that has not been planted by my Father shall be uprooted.” And how did the heavenly Father plant? Through prophets and apostles. And how did Satan plant? Through heretics and the ungodly. Let the plant of ungodliness be uprooted, and let no room be found in Satan’s place. Everything that opposes Christ’s power and rises against it is torn down. Darkness that contends against the light is driven away by the light. But let us come to what lies before us.

The Giver of Life rebuked the cities: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Let the Gospel say now as well: “Woe to you, Arius! Woe to you, Macedonius! Woe to you, Eunomius! For if the preaching proclaimed among you had been proclaimed in Sodom, perhaps they would have marveled at the Savior, glorified the Benefactor, and recognized the Creator.” Indeed, brothers, we ought not to be angry with the schismatics, but to mourn over them. Listen to the Scripture that says: “Mourn for the dead for seven days, but for the fool and the ungodly all their days.” And who is the fool, the one without understanding? Let David tell us: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” It is not only the pagan who says, “There is no God,” but these people also. For outwardly they say that there is a God, but in practice they do not say that God exists. When a heretic says that Christ is God, but does not consider him God by nature, he says it only in words and has denied it in practice. For they say that Christ is God, but not by nature as the Father is, since the nature of the one is different from the nature of the other. When someone denies in his heart and mind the honor of the Son’s divinity, even though he calls him God, he does not consider him God, for he effaces the true image of divinity with destructive [?].

And now, what should be said about this? Prophecy was spring, as I said before, and the Gospel was the harvest. But do not let the words I spoke yesterday seem strange to you: that the time of the prophets was the time of spring and sowing, and that of the Gospel was the time of summer and harvest. For there are other harvests as well. The prophets sowed, and the apostles reaped after Christ’s coming. Again, God sows, and the angels reap. The apostles became the reapers of the prophets’ sowing, and the angels become the reapers of the Giver of Life’s preaching. The prophets sowed knowledge of things to come; they also sowed the coming of Christ, announcing it beforehand. Christ’s apostles reaped. Christ sowed beforehand the hope of the resurrection. The prophets also sowed the future coming of the Giver of Life. And Christ sowed the future resurrection of the dead and his own second coming. That the apostles became the reapers of the first sowing, and that the angels become the reapers of the second, is stated in his own words: “Behold, the sower went out to sow good seed. Weeds also sprang up alongside it.” And, to cut it short: “At harvest time I will tell the reapers, ‘Gather the weeds separately, and the wheat separately.’” When the disciples asked what the parable meant, he said: “The field is the world, and the one who sowed is the Son of Man. The good seed is the children of the kingdom, and the weeds are the children of the evil one. The harvest is the end of the world.”

And Zechariah does not show the punishments inflicted by the scythe without reason; the Greek calls it a sickle. He says, “I saw a flying scythe, and I said to the angel who was speaking to me, ‘Lord, what is this?’ And he said, ‘These are the curses that go out over the face of the whole earth and consume the liar and his house and everything that belongs to him.’ Why not a sword, a spear, or an arrow, but a sickle? Because a sickle is kept for the harvest, and the reapers, the angels, are sent out and gather the grain. Then the whole world can be seen harvested at once. And from where will they reap? They will draw them out of the graves. They will not cut them apart, but join together those who have been cut apart. Now bodies have been sown in the fields like seeds, as Paul also says: “So it is with the resurrection of the dead: it is sown in corruption and rises without corruption.” And because they were sown in graves, they will be reaped from graves. He says, “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from the ends of heaven to the ends of the earth.” You will recognize these words in David: “Gather his holy ones to him.” They will gather everyone and bring them together in one place.

Everyone will rise, but some will be placed before the dreadful judgment seat as those condemned to punishment, while others will be caught up to meet the Lord as holy ones. Just as, when a king enters, a condemned person does not dare to appear before the king, while the dignitaries and those held in honor go out to meet him, so also, when the Son of God comes from heaven and appears, the holy ones are caught up into the heights. Thus it will seem that they are coming with him. Just as those who go out to meet a king and return with him seem to have been with him all along, so also, when the holy ones are caught up to meet the Giver of Life, it will seem that they are descending from heaven with him. And who bears witness to this? Paul: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet of God. And the dead will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.” See: they go out to meet him and come with him.

And pay attention to these wonders. In this world, those who go out to meet kings go in their own chariots and on their own horses. But the Giver of Life himself sends heavenly envoys—not chariots and horses, but chariots of cloud, his very own. And why do you marvel that Elijah was taken up in fiery chariots, while the apostles and others, one by one, are taken up in chariots of cloud? Do not consider the fiery chariot more honorable than the chariot of cloud. At that time, envoys were sent to the prophet: fiery chariots and fiery horses. He ascended from these heavenly beings into heaven, and like a wheel he rolled upward from below into the heights. But at that time fiery chariots were indeed fitting, whereas afterward they are not fiery but made of cloud. Why? Because at that time the heavenly vessel still had some earthly needs, so that through the fiery chariots it might be renewed, cast off its earthly weight, and receive the lightness of angels; for from then on he was to dwell with the angels themselves. There the envoy was fiery, and here the envoy is made of cloud. For bodies rise without corruption, and therefore they ascend lightly into the cloud. And so that no one may think that we disparage the former and honor the latter, I said that the prophet was honored with fiery chariots, while those who are caught up to meet Christ ascend on clouds. For clouds are the chariots of the holy God. And hear David: he says, “He established his upper chambers upon the waters and made the clouds his means of travel.” He honors the saints with his own chariots. Hear Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and will come into Egypt.” See that he commands the saints to be honored with his own chariots and to go out to meet the Giver of Life.

And how will they go up? He himself makes it clear, for Paul never speaks on his own authority, as he also says: “You seek proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.” And what does he say? “We shall be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” And so half will be caught up, and half will be set before the fearsome judgment seat. As the Life-giver himself also says: “Truly I tell you, when the Son of Man comes, then, if two are in one bed, one will be taken and the other left. And if two are grinding at one mill, one will be lifted up and the other left.” And the apostles say to him: “Where, Lord?” And the Lord says: “Where the body is, there the eagles will gather.” Why eagles? Because they will be caught up into the heights.

What does it mean that two will be in one bed, and one will be taken and the other left, and that two will grind at one mill, and one will be lifted up and the other remain? There is no need here to explain one thing through another by an allegory; rather, the interpretation is plain. Scripture calls the ease of this world a bed, and the severe suffering of those who toil a mill: they remain bewildered, as though in a mill, amid various afflictions, passing from groaning to groaning and from poverty to poverty. And let Moses bear witness that Scripture calls severe suffering a mill. He says: “The angel went out and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the royal throne, to the firstborn of the captive who was at the mill.”

For this reason Isaiah also spoke reproachfully to the ruler of the Babylonians: “You said,” he says, “‘I am, and I shall remain forever’”—meaning, “I shall reign forever.” “For this reason childlessness will come upon you. Take a mill and grind flour.” For he said: “I shall hold my power and kingship forever, and I shall not see widowhood.” And he brings him down from the royal throne and binds him to the mill. “Take a mill,” he says, “grind flour; cross the river”—meaning, “You will wander about suffering and stumbling.”

And since beds signify rest and the mill signifies toil, the Life-giver makes clear that both among those who do not toil and among those who live at ease, some will be righteous and some sinful. Two will be in a bed: one, who is worthy of the faith, will be lifted up, and the other will belong to the demons. “And two,” he says, “will grind at one mill; one will be taken up and the other remain.” The disciples asked about this same meaning and said: “Lord, where will they be lifted up?” He says to them: “Where my body is”—meaning, “Where my coming will be.”

And he rightly said, “the body,” for he will be revealed in the body. Although the body was covered with divinity and suffused with the immortal root, [?] immortality itself, it did not lose its form. Rather, the form of the body remains, suffused and immersed in life. Let us bring forward an example of this. Although it may be obscure and faint, nevertheless, even in something small one can discern at least a few traces of something great. Take iron and plunge it into a fiery furnace, and see what it was like before it was plunged into the fire: dark in appearance and cold to the touch. After entering the fire, it is bright to look at and hot when examined. It has not ceased to be iron, but has received something beyond its own nature. Although it has become radiant, it has not departed from its own shape. Whatever shape you plunge into the furnace, that same shape appears: whether round, triangular, square, or whatever it may be, it does not change its shape. Only its color takes on the color of the fire. Likewise, the Lord’s holy body, worthy of worship, was suffused with the immortal root of godliness and immersed in life, and has clothed itself with divinity—not merely outwardly, but, like the iron, inwardly and outwardly. Yet its form remains uncorrupted, to the glory of those who believe and the shame of those who despise it.

And have you not seen how, when people return from a foreign land after a long time, their relatives seek a identifying sign—not some sign of their splendor, even if they return in splendor, but a sign of their former life, to determine whether this is truly the same person? They do not look so closely at their clothes as at the shape of their eyebrows, the distinguishing marks of their hands, and their hair—whether it is [?] or curly. Bodily defects become a herald identifying the unfamiliar person. For this reason, he does not wish to save the saints through divinity, but through the features of the body, so that they may look and see that he is indeed the one who was not believed before Caiaphas, was judged by Pilate, and went up on the cross. Thus his appearance will bear witness to the struggle against God, and his glory will reveal the truth. [?] God, how Peter will rejoice, and the apostles will dance and walk about, and say to one another: “This is our God! This is the one who was once crucified among us! This is the one who was once despised for our sake! Look at his features; pay attention to his eyes!”

And who had said this beforehand? Isaiah. “In the last days,” he says, “they will say, ‘Here is our God, in whom we hoped,’ and they will rejoice, and they will see eye to eye when the Lord has mercy on Zion.” This means that he will appear openly, directly before their eyes. The righteous rejoice and recognize their Lord; the wicked mourn when they recognize the one they despised. For if someone here in this world has wronged another, and then falls from honor and sees the person he wronged in authority, he becomes afraid and trembles, wondering whether that person will remember what happened and call the insult to mind. He devises all sorts of ways to calm his anger: can he persuade him personally, or through friends? But how will you persuade your Lord? Through the martyrs whom you slandered, or through the apostles whom you dishonored, whose names you defamed—the names of Matthew and Bartholomew—saying, ‘What do they have in common with Plato? How do they compare with Aristotle?’ Now you despise their names, and then you will run to seek shelter under their intercession—with what eyes, with what boldness? But do not think you can persuade him. Will you resort to flight? Will you not listen to David: ‘Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence?’ And if there is nowhere to flee, you poor, miserable person, learn to flee to him for refuge. Those who realize that they will not escape the punishments imposed by judges, as the laws rightly require, have only one refuge left: to appeal to the king and have the penalty of their torments removed by royal favor. Therefore David too, recognizing the remorse for his sins that tormented him, and that he deserved punishment according to the commands of the law, flees from everyone and takes refuge in the Lord alone, saying, ‘You, Lord, are my hope and my refuge.’

And after saying, ‘Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,’ what does he say? ‘Then all the nations of the earth will mourn.’ Severe mourning will come upon unbelievers, just as great joy will come upon believers. And it was not only the giver of life who said this, but before him the prophet Zechariah: ‘Then the sun will set over the prophets, and the moon will be darkened. Then they will see the one whom they pierced.’ This means the one whom they nailed to the cross with nails. ‘Then the families will mourn separately: the families of the house of David separately, and their wives separately; the families of the house of Nathan separately, and their wives separately; every family separately, and their wives separately.’ Why does he speak of all the families, or why does he mention David and Nathan? Nathan was not one of the patriarchs, but belonged to David’s family. David had two powerful sons. Although he had many sons, two were distinguished: Solomon and Nathan. Joseph’s family descends from Nathan, and Mary’s family is from Solomon. Mary was of royal descent, and although Joseph too was of royal descent, he was not descended from Solomon, who received David’s throne, but from Nathan, the king’s brother. And because the disgrace of fighting against God was to fall upon them all, and especially upon his relatives, who did not recognize their own Savior, he says, ‘The family of David will mourn separately.’ And because Christ was descended from David according to the flesh, his relatives mourn over what a guarantor of salvation they have lost.

And now, so that we may not mourn but rejoice together and receive the crucified one with glory, let the Jews who raised the body of the Son of God upon the cross hear this, and the heretics who despised his divinity. The writings of the prophets and the apostles will be opened before Christ’s tribunal. Do you suppose that the prophets will not come to the tribunal, that the Jews will not stand bowed before Christ’s judgment seat, and that the heretics will not be stricken and brokenhearted at the fearful judgment? The Jews will be questioned: “Why did you deny him?” The heretics will be questioned: “Why did you blaspheme?” And what answer will they be able to give? But perhaps the Jew will say, “I heard from the prophets: ‘I am God, and besides me there is no other God. I am the first, and I am the last.’ We learned this from the prophet Isaiah, and what could we wretched people have done?” And he will say to the heretics, “And why did you blaspheme the Son? Why did you insult the glory of the Only-begotten?” Perhaps they too will say, “Peter taught us this way, and Paul instructed us this way: Christ is our peace, who made the two one and reconciled us to the Father, as a mediator between God and human beings. He proclaimed him as a mediator, and not as God, and we were deceived.”

Then the companies of the prophets will become angry, and the ranks of the apostles will be enraged. They will bring out the books. Isaiah will open his book and say, “See, Lord, how I became a defender of your anointing. Let the declarations that I spoke about you be read. Let the Jews hear them; let the Christians say whether the apostles proclaimed anything more than I did. Did I not know you, the only-begotten Son of God? Did I not proclaim beforehand: ‘A child was born to us; a son was given to us. And his name is called Messenger of the Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Glorious, Prince of Peace, Father of the world to come’? Are not the proclamation of divinity and the saving dispensation distinct from one another? At one time: ‘God, Mighty, Glorious, Prince of Peace’; at another: ‘Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,’ which translated means ‘God with us.’ Did I not also proclaim his sufferings: ‘He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and for the sins of the people he was handed over to death’? Did I not also proclaim his coming? Did I say, ‘A prophet is coming, and not God’? Just as the prophet Zechariah said, ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes, riding on a donkey,’ so I too said, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with power.’ None of the apostles became a herald of you as I did. They proclaimed you together with your flesh and gave occasion for blasphemy through ignorance. But I proclaimed your divinity fully: ‘Messenger of the Great Counsel, God, Mighty, Glorious, Prince of Peace, Father of the world to come.’ None of your apostles said this. I became your herald before the apostles. Let no one slander my writings.” Isaiah says this with a fervent mind, for he is bold and impartial, just as the Apostle says, “Isaiah is bold and says.”

And Moses too comes forward, who was dearer and more honorable to the Jews than God. Stepping into their midst, he too becomes an advocate. He begins to say, “You miserable and wretched people!” For Moses’ [?] are different; he rebukes them gently. “The man Moses,” it says, “was gentler than all human beings.” “Did I not already foretell the barrenness of your unbelief? Because you could not accept greater things, I said, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from your own people; listen to him. And every person who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed.’ And if you considered this a small thing, did I not proclaim the Trinity right at the beginning of the account of creation? Sometimes I said, ‘God said, Let there be light’; sometimes, ‘Let us make a human being according to the likeness of the image of our forms’; and sometimes, ‘Come, let us go down and divide their languages.’ Did I not write with my own hands that the Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon the people of Sodom and Gomorrah? Will I not grieve over your destruction? But I consider it better to disregard you and not stand against you [?].” And who will be a witness to this statement? The Lord himself, who said concerning the Jews, “Do you think that I will accuse you before the Father? There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you take pride. For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me, because he wrote about me.” And Daniel testifies that the books will be opened: “I watched as the Ancient of Days sat down, and his throne was like fire. I watched as thrones were cast down and books were opened.” They will say all these things concerning the Jews.

Let the heretics be called forward. Let Paul stand before them as their accuser, for he was slandered by their godless tongues. Let them also be called to account: “Where did you read that the Son is said to be inferior to the Father?” They say, “You and Peter taught this. He said, ‘Exalted at the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Spirit, he poured it out upon us.’ And again, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.’ ‘God made that Jesus both Lord and Christ.’ And you said, ‘God the Father, who raised him from the dead.’ And again, ‘I thank God through Jesus Christ.’ And you did not say, ‘[?],’ but, ‘Through him I thank God.’” Then let Paul open his mouth, which was never closed, who said, “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians.” And let him rebuke them: “Son of lawlessness, wicked seed, plant of unbelief, did I not proclaim the divinity of the Only-begotten? Did I not say, ‘Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever’? Did I not say, ‘He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’? Did I not say, ‘There is neither barbarian nor savage nor Scythian, but Christ is all and in all’? Did I not say, ‘He is the radiance of glory, the imprint of his being, and the image of the invisible God, who upholds everything by his power’?” And they say, “Did you not proclaim him as a man? Did you not proclaim Christ according to the flesh?” “But although I proclaimed Christ according to the flesh, I also said elsewhere, ‘Even though we knew Christ according to the flesh, we no longer know him in that way.’” Let Peter also come forward and say, “You read about my accommodation to the Gentiles and the Jews, but did you not read the great confession I made concerning Christ? For which confession did I receive the keys? Was it because I called Jesus a Nazarene? No, but because I said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ When I said, ‘He made him Lord and Christ,’ was it when the offspring was begotten of the Father?”

And now, be watchful, for the books and writings will be opened, and the King will sit, and the defenders of the truth will come forward, and the accusers will be put to shame. Let us act before the judgment. Before the King sits to judge, it is possible to win the Judge’s favor. Before the judgment, one can plead; before the fearsome judgment seat, there is no opportunity to make an appeal. May all of us appear blameless before the judgment seat of Christ, for his are glory and power forever. Amen.
